title: A New Look for LSU Libraries
subtitle: The redesign of lib.lsu.edu, before and after
credit: Designed and built by LSU Libraries, 2026. [Editor: names and departments]
intro: A library website is a reading room you can enter from anywhere. Over 2026 we rebuilt ours around three ideas: say less and show more, put the next step within reach, and let every reader set the page to suit them. Choose a gallery to see the pages side by side.

staff.title: A New Look for LSU Libraries: Staff Edition
staff.subtitle: The redesign of lib.lsu.edu, before and after, with notes for editors
staff.intro: A library website is a reading room you can enter from anywhere. Over 2026 we rebuilt ours around three ideas: say less and show more, put the next step within reach, and let every reader set the page to suit them. This edition adds four galleries for staff: how to build a guide and an exhibition, the standards behind the design, and how changes reach the site.

blocks.title: Why we changed it
blocks.body: The old site grew over fifteen years across several systems. Research guides lived in LibGuides, exhibitions on a separate blog, and each had its own menus, colours and type. Readers had to learn three websites to use one library.

blocks.title: What's different
blocks.body:
• One design. Guides, exhibitions and Special Collections now share one typeface, one grid and one set of controls.
  • The next step first. Today's hours, the search box and the way to request material come before the history and the policies.
  • Readable everywhere. Every page is built for the phone first and checked against WCAG 2.2 AA, the international accessibility standard.
  • Quieter motion. Movement is slow and purposeful, and it stops completely when you ask your device or the site to reduce motion.

blocks.title: How to read this exhibition
blocks.body: Each gallery shows a page before and after. Open a pair and drag the line to wipe between them, or choose Fade.

The Special Collections home page used to open with the library-wide search panel, a carousel and a purple wash over Hill Memorial Library. Hours appeared in the header, but the way in was a list of links. The new page opens on Hill itself. It says whether the building is open right now, shows the week's hours, and puts a search of the collections, along with the request sign-in, on the first screen. Below it, a Quick Start Guide walks through requesting material step by step.

blocks.body: Research guides used to live in LibGuides. Each tab was its own page, and the tab bar could run to three rows. Now a guide is a single page. Every former tab is a section, and the table of contents at the side follows you as you read, so the whole guide is one scroll and one search away. Numbered steps, decision trees and side notes are set as type, not as boxes. Links to databases say when they need an LSU login.

blocks.body: Online exhibitions used to be blog posts or pages of small pictures. The Audubon exhibition showed 600-pixel close-ups, and Occult Science used 1,000-pixel scans. Each new exhibition opens like a gallery entrance: a title page, then one room at a time. Plates are shown whole, from scans of up to 4K, and open full screen with zoom. Where Audubon's drawing and the printed plate survive, you can lay one over the other and wipe between them, the same way this exhibition compares its screenshots.

blocks.body:
The gear icon at the top of every page opens Settings:

  • Reading colours: thirteen page and text colour schemes, light and dark, each keeping text at 4.5:1 contrast or better.
  • Text size: up to 150%.
  • Easy-to-read font: Atkinson Hyperlegible.
  • Text spacing: more space between lines, words and letters.
  • Underline all links.
  • High contrast.
  • Reduce motion, and pause background videos.

Your choices are saved on your device and apply across the site. The clock, chat and person icons beside the gear open today's hours, Ask Us and your library accounts without leaving the page.

• A guide is a Modular page with Type = guide. Each former LibGuide tab becomes a section, and each box becomes a block.
  • Block headings are Heading 3 and appear in the table of contents. Inside a block, use Heading 4.
  • A numbered list becomes steps; start an item with bold text to give the step a title. A bulleted list with a nested list becomes a decision tree.
  • Add Resources first, then pick them by title. Paste the plain address and tick "Requires LSU login"; don't paste libezp links.
  • Don't add "Next / Previous" text; the table of contents handles navigation.
  • A paragraph containing only [request-paths] draws the Special Collections request diagram.

• One gallery per room. Its opening can be Cover (the lead image full screen), Full screen then pan, or Compact.
  • Story or Wall display. On a wall, each entry's first image is a tile. An entry whose image group holds exactly two images becomes a comparison: caption them "Before" and "After" (or "Drawing" and "Proof"), as in this exhibition.
  • Images: upload the largest file you have. The site makes 640–2560px WebP copies and never sends the original. Set a focal point for cropped leads.
  • Alt text lives on the media item. Describe what the image shows and why it matters, not "image of".
  • An Image block with no image shows only to editors, as a reminder.
  • Captions that say "plate 40" give the wall its plate numbers and A–Z / Plate sorting.

• WCAG 2.2 AA throughout: 4.5:1 text contrast, visible focus, labelled controls, reduced motion respected in every script.
  • Built for phones first and checked at 320, 768, 1024 and 1440px.
  • Speed: images lazy-load at fixed sizes (no layout shift), and scripts load only on the pages that use them.
  • Visual rules: Swiss-style grid, one hairline weight for every rule, hover colour in 0.2s and out 0.5s, Font Awesome 5 icons only.

• Content: edit in Drupal; it's live when published.
  • Design: changes are reviewed, then deployed to lib.lsu.edu and passed on to the staging site. [Editor: who to contact, and how to report a problem]
  • Where the old pages went: LibGuides [Editor: redirect plan], exhibitions blog [Editor].
